before.name: Tyrolean Schuhplattler (slap-dance with music)
before.lineage: Tyrolean Schuhplattler folk-dance-and-music tradition of the Austrian Tyrol, South Tyrol (Italy), and Bavarian Alps, in which male dancers perform synchronized choreography involving rhythmic slapping of thighs, knees, and shoe-soles in characteristic accelerating patterns, accompanied by Stubenmusik chamber-ensemble of zither, hammered dulcimer (Hackbrett), accordion, double-bass, and voice. Performance contexts span the Heimatabend folkloric-evening tourist-demonstrations, village-festival celebrations, and the canonical Schuhplattlerverein dance-association competitions. Distinguished from broader German Alpine music by Schuhplattler's specific male-percussive-choreographic register.

before.name: Medieval Latin chant and Notre Dame organum
before.lineage: Medieval Western European liturgical music tradition spanning monophonic Gregorian chant (canonized late ninth century, eight church modes, Latin liturgical text) and the early-polyphonic organum that emerged from it. Ninth-century parallel organum (the chant doubled at the fifth or fourth, with optional octave doubling); twelfth-century melismatic organum (the chant slowed to drone-tone in the lower voice while the upper voice elaborates ornamentally over each chant pitch). The Notre Dame school, Paris, c.1160-1250, codified the rhythmic-modes system and expanded to three-and-four-voice organum: Léonin (c.1135-1201), credited with the Magnus Liber Organi (the great book of organum), set the two-voice canonical repertoire; Pérotin (fl. c.1200), expanded to three and four voices and composed canonical large-scale organum-quadruplum settings of Viderunt omnes (1198) and Sederunt principes. Cantus firmus practice: the chant melody remains in one voice (typically the tenor) while the other voices counterpoint above. Anonymous IV (English theorist, c.1270s, his treatise survives in a thirteenth-century Bury St Edmunds manuscript) preserves the attribution of these works to Léonin and Pérotin. Distinguished from Renaissance sacred polyphony by limited-voice-count and modal-not-tonal harmonic vocabulary; distinguished from Byzantine chant by Latin-language and Roman-rite cantus-firmus framing; distinguished from Old Roman chant by Frankish-redacted melodic-formulae lineage

before.name: Jewish Kaddish mourner recitation
before.lineage: The Kaddish is a doxology in Aramaic and Hebrew central to Jewish liturgy, its best-known form the Mourner's Kaddish (Kaddish Yatom) recited by the bereaved during the eleven months of mourning and on the yahrzeit. The text sanctifies God's name and, notably, contains no mention of death; it is delivered by the mourner in a rapid, low, rhythmic spoken flow, with the congregation answering the responsorial refrain 'Yehei shmei rabba mevarach.' Its melodic contours vary by rite (Ashkenazi, Sephardi, Yemenite) but the mourner's form leans toward recitation rather than song. The tradition is documented across the siddur manuscript tradition and centuries of synagogue practice.

before.name: Renaissance sacred polyphony (1450-1600)
before.lineage: Renaissance European sacred-music tradition c.1450-1600, the mass-cycle and motet repertoire of the Franco-Flemish and Italian schools. Canonical compositional features: imitative counterpoint with successive voice-entries on the same melodic subject; smooth melodic voice-leading with stepwise motion and small leaps; controlled dissonance through suspension-and-resolution; modal scales transitioning gradually into tonal practice; a cappella ideal with optional organ accompaniment for liturgical performance. Canonical composers: Josquin des Prez (Franco-Flemish, c.1450-1521, founding figure of the imitative-mass tradition); Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina (Roman, 1525-1594, Missa Papae Marcelli 1567 the Counter-Reformation touchstone for the smoothness-and-clarity ideal); Thomas Tallis (English, c.1505-1585, the forty-voice motet Spem in alium c.1570); William Byrd (English, c.1543-1623, Mass for Four Voices); Orlande de Lassus (Flemish, 1532-1594); Tomás Luis de Victoria (Spanish, 1548-1611). Geographical centers: Cambrai, Antwerp, Rome (Cappella Sistina), Venice (San Marco), London (Chapel Royal). Distinguished from medieval organum by full imitative counterpoint and tempered-meantone tuning vocabulary; distinguished from Baroque sacred polyphony by absence of basso continuo and absence of operatic-aria stylistic vocabulary; distinguished from Orthodox liturgical chant by Latin-text Roman-rite (vs Slavonic / Greek Orthodox-rite) liturgical framework

before.name: Solomon Islands panpipe ensemble
before.lineage: Solomon Islands panpipe ensemble tradition of the Are'are people of southern Malaita island and adjacent Solomons communities, featuring large coordinated ensembles of stopped-bamboo-pipes-arranged-in-rafts played in interlocking hocketed polyphonic patterns. The au tahana (raft-panpipe) and au kuita (bundle-panpipe) instrumental categories support distinct repertoire layers. Performance contexts span feast-day celebrations, mourning-rituals, and (post-1978 independence) international-festival and recording-circuit work through the canonical Narasirato Pan Pipers ensemble formed in the 1990s. The genre is one of the most internationally circulated Melanesian musical traditions through twentieth-century ethnomusicological recording.

before.name: Asturian gaita (Iberian Celtic bagpipe)
before.lineage: Asturian gaita Iberian Celtic-bagpipe tradition of Asturias (northern Spain), the canonical Asturian regional-folk-music instrumental signature. The gaita asturiana is a mouth-blown single-drone bagpipe distinct from the larger Galician gaita gallega and the Scottish Highland pipes in tuning and ornament-vocabulary. Performance: solo gaita or gaita-and-tambor (drum-pair) accompanying voice, dance, or solo instrumental display. Repertoire spans foliada wedding-celebration repertoire, vaqueirada cattle-herder dance-music, and the canonical Asturian-Celtic revival-period compositions of the late-twentieth century. Distinguished from Galician gaita gallega by Asturian-specific tuning and ornamental conventions. The Asturian Cultural Council and the parallel Galician Real Academia de la Gaita anchor institutional preservation.

before.name: Old-time radio announcer
before.lineage: American network-radio announcer style of the 1930s-50s NBC and CBS era, delivered in projected, precisely articulated diction — often the cultivated Mid-Atlantic ('transatlantic') accent taught in period broadcast and elocution training — into RCA 44 and 77 ribbon microphones. Staff and program announcers such as Don Wilson (The Jack Benny Program), Harry von Zell, Ken Carpenter, and Milton Cross (the Metropolitan Opera broadcasts) defined the register across variety-show openings, drama introductions, station identifications, and live commercial reads; Orson Welles's 1938 Mercury Theatre on the Air 'War of the Worlds' broadcast famously exploited the authority this announcer voice carried. The sound is inseparable from the period transmission chain: ribbon mic, tube electronics, and bandwidth-limited live AM air or transcription disc.

before.name: Documentary voiceover
before.lineage: Authoritative scripted narration read over documentary picture, descending from 1930s-40s newsreel narration such as Westbrook Van Voorhis's reads for The March of Time into postwar television nature and history documentary. Canonical exemplars include David Attenborough's intimate-authoritative BBC natural-history narration (Life on Earth, 1979, through the Planet Earth series), David McCullough's narration of Ken Burns's The Civil War (1990) and Peter Coyote's later Burns work, and Morgan Freeman's March of the Penguins (2005) as the popular touchstone of the warm 'voice of God' register. The performer reads alone to picture in a dry, treated studio, balancing measured pacing and low, resonant delivery against the score and location-sound bed.
before.recipe: classic mid-1930s documentary voiceover, spoken Word, narration branch audiobook narration old-time radio announcer. vocal fry, breath veiled tone, slow rate, interlocked note trading. treated studio.
